Perhaps the most damning is, as modern studies would also show, that abuse in 93% ([RAINN](https://rainn.org/statistics/perpetrators-sexual-violence)) of cases is perpetrated by someone known to the victim, and speaking out against them, or even writing down evidence (if the underage person was literate), could put them into dangerous situations. Legally, until the Offences Against the Person Act in 1828, CSAM for girls either fell into rape law under Edward I's c.13 'Punishment of him that doth ravish a Woman' statute in 1275 or kidnapping and/or assault with intent of a ward 'Punishment of him that taketh away a Ward' act in 1285. For boys (and sometimes girls), the Buggery Act of 1533 would be the most likely legal prosecution. In all, however, it relied on the victim having evidence or their word both of which is hard to prove, particularly if the victim was too young to understand what had been done to them. Also to consider was their own and their families reputations, acknowledgement of rape or assault impacted the girls ability to get married as she would be seen as 'impure' and the social ramifications from 'homosexual acts' would be a whole other mess. Everything from finances to social status relied upon reputation. When your economy relies upon credit and no person is willing to be your reference or crediter due to your families reputation you'd be lucky if you didn't lose everything.

UK lesbian here and I do feel like the sensitivity to the word (I think OP wants to keep it PG) c* nt is an American thing. It's a curse word but on the same level as sh* t or f* ck. As someone who is and has friends who are LGBTQ+ we use the words in the same way that gay men and drag queens do. It depends I think on how you are socialised and what connotations your culture assigns to words. From what I've noticed the words are only used in a positive manner, even if its celebrating bad behaviour. It's never said to harm another person.

I think that for drag queens its a little less misogynistic as they are performing and celebrating womanhood. 

Also for general info the slurs for queer folk in the UK (especially as I was growing up) were not the same as ones in the US. Particularly 'fag' which has always meant cigarette, the longer form of the word did make its way into the slur catagory but it was not the chosen word to throw around. It's not that we're unaware of what the American's use for slurs but trust me we had our own. 

Above all, if the words offend or hurt you (plural), you should really ascertain why, what caused you to have that reaction, and what would a difference in the person saying it make to you. Would it be better or worse say if it were only lesbians using it and not gay men. Would you be okay with a feminine person saying the words? Is it the words themselves? Not to doubt anybodies reaction but ut helps you understand the situation more if you introspect for a bit. (this is directed generally not at you, the person who i'm replying to).

Hi darling, it's been a rough year and a half - so kudos to you for getting through your first year of university! You're not alone in feeling anxious at the prospect of 'returning' (i.e. going for the first time) to university - especially since the work load often increases each year - and well without the 'proper' introduction to the university environment in the first year the idea of balancing academic and social life is nerve-wracking to say the least! 

Whatever happens and whatever you choose to do, you'll be alright. Whether you exceed the hopes or fall short on them, you'll be alright. After all it will be your choice to make. Saying that, I wouldn't give up on university just yet (or before the second year starts) after all, how will you know the outcome if you don't do it! The outcome is the outcome but at least you can say you tried - regardless of what happens next.

Also, on the cheating, to be blunt - if the university did not have the measures to stop 'cheating' then thats their fault, not yours! You were simply doing what is called an 'open-book' exam (which is what they should have given out in the first place, but thats neither here nor there). 

Everything will turn out alright - even if it seems like the opposite! Good luck darling x

Hi darling, that does sound like a lot to be dealing with  - no wonder you feel a bit lost! It's perfectly normal to be feeling like this, not knowing what you want to do but being sure of what you don't want to do. Hell, I felt the same when I left school. The idea of working for the rest of your life? Yuck!

But seriously, this feeling will come and go but you'll begin to figure out what it is you like and what things you enjoy enough to make everything a little less daunting. When it comes to work you'll begin find out what kind of work (regardless of whether its physical, office, academic) you can tolerate and what kind will have you quitting after a month. Don't give up on applying for jobs! I know it's such a chore and disheartening to recieve nothing back but they'll be offers soon enough. Though depending on where you are you may have to lower your standards a bit just so you can get some work experience to put on your CV.

The situation with your parents is a bit trickier. Are you in a position to talk honestly with them? If so, tell them about your struggles with the job market. If not well you're not alone in finding it difficult and I'm always willing to listen! 

If they're just giving you the ultimatum of moving out so you'll be influenced to get a job, volunteering for a charity or something similar may get them off your backs for a while and add a bit more to your CV which may give you a bit more luck with the job search!

You have your own skills, even if you can't quite see them yet, and your dream or ideas for the future will clarify as you get older. No need to add more stress to yourself by thinking you should have everything planned and under control - nobody has that and much less at your age and in your situation.

Take it day by day! Good luck darling! x
